passages.title: The Return of the Red Kite
paras: For anyone driving along the motorway between London and Oxford today, the sight of a large, rust-coloured bird of prey circling above the fields is unremarkable. Yet only a few decades ago, the red kite had vanished entirely from England. Its return is widely regarded as one of the most successful wildlife reintroductions in British history, and it offers useful lessons for conservationists working with other species.

In the Middle Ages, red kites were common in towns as well as in the countryside. They were valued as scavengers: by feeding on rubbish and dead animals in the streets, they helped to keep settlements clean, and for a time it was even an offence to harm them. Attitudes changed from the sixteenth century onwards, when laws encouraged people to kill birds and animals that were thought to threaten crops and livestock. Later, the rise of large shooting estates in the nineteenth century made matters worse. Gamekeepers, whose job was to protect young pheasants and grouse, saw all birds of prey as competitors and shot, trapped or poisoned them in large numbers.

By the end of the nineteenth century, the red kite had been wiped out in England and Scotland. A small population survived only in the remote valleys of central Wales, where a few local landowners and volunteers protected nests from egg collectors. Even there, numbers remained dangerously low for most of the twentieth century, partly, it is thought, because the Welsh birds produced relatively few young.

In 1989, conservation organisations began a programme to bring the species back to England and Scotland. Rather than taking birds from the fragile Welsh population, they collected young kites from nests in Spain, and later from Sweden, where the species was still relatively common. The birds were released at carefully chosen sites, including the Chiltern Hills north-west of London. Before release, each bird was kept for several weeks in a large cage, or aviary, so that it could become familiar with its new surroundings. Each was also fitted with a small radio transmitter, which allowed scientists to follow its movements.

The choice of the Chilterns was not accidental. The area combined open farmland, where the birds could search for food, with patches of woodland that provided safe places to nest. Equally important, there were relatively few shooting estates nearby, which reduced the risk of illegal persecution. The results exceeded expectations. Within a few years the released birds had begun to breed, and their offspring spread steadily outwards. Today, red kites are a familiar sight across much of southern England, and the total UK population is estimated to be in the thousands of breeding pairs.

Not every release site was as successful. In some parts of northern Scotland, kite numbers grew far more slowly than expected, and examinations of dead birds revealed that many had died from eating poisoned bait that had been put out illegally to kill foxes or crows. The contrast between regions shows that habitat alone is not enough: a reintroduction depends just as much on how local people behave.

The red kite's comeback has also created some unexpected problems. In certain villages, residents began putting out meat in their gardens to attract the birds, and in some areas this has led to large groups of kites gathering over houses. Some people worry that the birds have become too dependent on human food, while others complain that kites occasionally snatch food from people's hands. Conservationists generally advise against feeding the birds, pointing out that there is plenty of natural food in the countryside.

Nevertheless, the project is now used as a model elsewhere. Supporters argue that its success came from three things: long-term funding, careful scientific monitoring and, above all, the support of farmers and landowners, who were consulted from the very beginning. Without that support, they say, even the best-planned release would have failed.

passages.title: The Box That Changed the World
paras: For most of history, loading a ship was a slow, labour-intensive business. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bundles of every shape and size, and each item had to be lifted on board by teams of dock workers, known in Britain as dockers and in the United States as longshoremen. Fitting thousands of differently shaped objects into a ship's hold was a skilled job, and it could take longer to load and unload a vessel than to sail it across an ocean. Damage was common, and so was theft: dock work had a reputation for goods going missing somewhere between the ship and the warehouse.

The man usually credited with changing this was Malcom McLean, an American who owned a large trucking company rather than a shipping line. According to a story he often told, the idea came to him while he sat in his truck at a port in the 1930s, waiting for hours while his cargo was moved onto a ship piece by piece. Why, he wondered, could the whole trailer not simply be lifted on board? Two decades later he put the idea into practice. In April 1956, a converted oil tanker called the Ideal-X sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying 58 metal containers on its deck.

The economic effects were immediate. McLean calculated that loading cargo in the traditional way cost around $5.86 per ton, while loading the Ideal-X had cost less than 16 cents per ton. Because containers could be packed at the factory and sealed, they also reduced theft and damage, which in turn lowered insurance costs. Ships spent days rather than weeks in port, which meant that each vessel could make more voyages a year.

Not everyone welcomed the change. For dock workers, containerisation threatened the jobs on which whole communities depended. A task that had once required a gang of twenty men could now be done by a single crane operator. Unions in several countries organised strikes, and in some ports long negotiations were needed before agreements were reached that protected the incomes of existing workers, even though fewer new workers would be hired.

A further obstacle was technical. In the early years, each shipping company designed its own containers, and the boxes of one company often could not be stacked on the ships, lorries or trains of another. A container that suited one firm's equipment might be a few inches too long for its rival's. It was not until the late 1960s that international standards for container sizes and corner fittings were agreed, allowing any box to be handled at any port in the world. The 20-foot container became the basic unit of measurement for the industry, and the capacity of ships is still expressed in 'twenty-foot equivalent units'.

Once standardisation was in place, the container transformed world trade. Because transport became so cheap, it was no longer necessary for factories to be close to their customers. Manufacturers could buy parts from one country, assemble them in another and sell the finished products on a third continent. Some economists now argue that the container did more to encourage globalisation than all the trade agreements signed in the same period.

The new system also had less visible consequences. Container ports need vast areas of flat land for storing boxes and deep water for giant ships, so cargo handling moved away from the old harbours in city centres to new sites, often many miles away. In cities such as London and New York, the traditional docks closed, and the neighbourhoods around them lost their main source of employment. Some of these areas were later redeveloped as offices and expensive housing, but for many former dock workers the change came too late.

passages.title: The Value of Boredom
paras: Boredom has a poor reputation. Parents try to protect children from it, employers see it as a threat to productivity, and an entire industry of apps, streaming services and games competes to make sure that we never have to experience it. Yet in recent years a number of psychologists have begun to argue that boredom is not simply an unpleasant state to be avoided. Some go further, suggesting that it may perform a useful function – and that our increasing ability to escape it could be doing us harm.

Part of the difficulty in studying boredom is defining it. Researchers generally agree that it involves a desire to be engaged in some satisfying activity combined with an inability to find one. This distinguishes it from relaxation, in which a person is content to do nothing, and from apathy, in which the desire to act is itself missing. Boredom, in other words, is not a lack of feeling but an uncomfortable state of wanting – and, like hunger or pain, it may exist to push us towards a change of behaviour.

How strongly people wish to avoid that discomfort was shown in a well-known series of experiments published in 2014. Participants were asked to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. Many found the experience unpleasant. More strikingly, when given the option of pressing a button that delivered a mild electric shock, a considerable number chose to shock themselves rather than simply sit with their thoughts – even though, earlier in the study, they had said they would pay money to avoid such a shock. Men were considerably more likely than women to press the button.

If boredom is so unwelcome, what might be its value? One answer comes from research on creativity. In a study carried out in Britain, one group of volunteers was given a deliberately dull task – copying numbers out of a telephone directory – before being asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. A second group went straight to the creative task. The volunteers who had been bored first produced more ideas, and the effect was even stronger for a third group who had only read the numbers rather than copying them. The researchers suggested that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows unusual connections to be made.

This explanation fits with a broader body of work on what is sometimes called the 'default mode' of the brain, a pattern of activity that appears when a person is not focused on the outside world. During these periods, the brain is far from idle: it seems to be reviewing memories, imagining the future and making sense of experience. If every quiet moment is immediately filled with a phone or a screen, the argument goes, this kind of internal processing is crowded out.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that boredom is always beneficial. Chronic boredom – a frequent, long-lasting tendency to feel bored – has been linked to a range of problems, including poor performance at school, overeating and risky behaviour. In such cases, boredom seems less a spur to creativity than a sign that something in a person's life or environment needs to change. Nor does the creativity research show that bored people produce better ideas, only more of them; whether those ideas are useful is a separate question.

In my view, the most reasonable conclusion lies somewhere between the extremes. The occasional experience of boredom is not a problem to be solved but a signal worth listening to. When we feel bored, we are being told that our current activity is not meeting our needs. The healthy response is neither to suffer in silence nor to reach automatically for distraction, but to ask what we actually want to be doing. Children, in particular, may benefit from being left to find their own entertainment from time to time, since learning to cope with empty time is itself a skill.

What seems clear is that the technology which allows us to avoid boredom so easily has arrived far faster than our understanding of its effects. It would be foolish to blame smartphones for every modern problem. But it would be equally foolish to assume that a mind which is never allowed to be bored loses nothing in the process.
